assumptions: The material is the original v12 text (round 1) or the spec copy (later rounds); cross-part references outside the targets may be named under missing_inputs.
obligations.criterion: Supported when every Control rule has a matching model behaviour (or a stated reason it is not modelled) and no path is found by which permitted writes make a not-acceptable artifact accepted or published. Violated when a concrete inconsistency or such a path is shown, with locators.
evidence_requirements: model run output or attack script result
obligations.question: Control layer and reference model: are the control rules of the Control part consistent with the reference model (Appendix A), and can the main Agent, using only the writes the Control part allows (contracts, facts by the permitted writers, admission requests, publish), cause an artifact that should not be accepted to be accepted or published?

missing_inputs: Methods part (Methods 2.1/2.2/2.4: post-hoc correction rules and confirmation semantics referenced by Control 4.4)
Delivery part (Delivery 2.3 definition of attested, 1.2 capabilities, 3.1 adapter mapping)
History part (rationale of earlier rounds; not supplied to reviewers by design)
answers.reasoning: I read the Control part and Core in full and the reference model's derivation, admission and test code. I traced each Control rule to its model function and ran the model: 86/86 scenarios passed and 39/39 mutations were killed. Most rules match the model: the closed format, the strictness order, effective contracts and lapse, execution state, producer and owning step, currency, checks, freeze items 1-5, accepted, admission items 1-6, reuse and publish. I then wrote attack scripts (attacks.py) that use only the writes the main Agent is allowed to make: contracts, freezes, admission requests and publish, with B and C acting honestly. Four of the five attacks succeed in the model, and the spec text sanctions the same outcome. (1) A revert needs a human (Control 1.2 'content changes' row; 4.2 binding). A cosmetic change that is not a literal revert gets around this. If the change reproduces an earlier, already-seen digest (deterministic step), or reproduces it in an unchecked upstream step, that earlier draw is bound and published again at T3C with no human decision. (2) A non-upstream check input is resolved to 'bound, or else the latest current artifact' (Control 5.2), and no rule requires it to be ok or to stay current. So a required check can be counted when it was evaluated against a held reference artifact, which failed its own required check, or against a reference artifact that was later invalidated. The target is then accepted and published. (3) For the rule that rejects new attempts while one is unknown, the model keys the 'same side effect' of a check attempt on its full identity, which includes the resolved check inputs. Control 3 keys it on check x criterion x target, so the model admits a second check attempt that the spec would reject.

evidence.requirement: model run output or attack script result

findings.claim: The rule that a revert needs a human can be bypassed with a cosmetic content change. A program, environment or external-dependency value that differs from the old one but deterministically reproduces an earlier, already-seen artifact digest (in the deliverable step, or in an unchecked upstream step) does not 'revive' any earlier attempt's identity, so the contract takes effect automatically. The new producer is then the earliest current producer of the old digest, so it becomes the representative producer and its binding sequence number is new. The old artifact's earlier check results, including its confirmation on S1, are bound to the digest and still count. The agent can therefore choose among several seen and confirmed draws, which the spec says needs human approval, and publish the chosen one at T3C. In the upstream variant the deliverable step is not even recomputed, so check-before-recompute does not apply. The spec's claim 'after several artifacts of a step have been seen, only the newest current one binds without a human' is false under the spec's own definitions.
findings.element: Control 1.2 'content changes' row (revert defined only as reviving an earlier attempt's identity) together with Control 4.2 representative producer/binding sequence number; model revives() and best_producer()
findings.evidence_text: attacks.py a1 and a2: literal revert -> pending_approval; cosmetic revert -> effective; bound(reco)=X1, achieved T3C, publish succeeds, len(decisions)=0. Possible fixes: define a revert by the reproduced artifact digest, i.e. any producer of a digest already produced by an earlier attempt of that step under a different identity does not re-bind it without a human; or keep the binding sequence number at the earliest producer of the digest.

findings.claim: A required check's result counts even when a declared check input that is not an upstream of the target is not ok. When the input step has no bound version, C resolves the input to the 'latest current artifact', which can be held: it failed its own required check. The input can also become invalidated after the check. Nothing in 4.3 makes the target's check result depend on the input's ok status or currency. As a result, a target whose required check was evaluated against a failed or superseded reference is accepted and published. Control 5.2 says such inputs are bound 'like consumed inputs', but consumed inputs must be current and bound for the consumer to be ok (4.2 upstream state), so the analogy does not hold and the case is not covered.
findings.element: Control 5.2 resolution rule for check inputs and Control 4.3 counting condition; model check_inputs_for() and check_inputs_hold()
findings.evidence_text: attacks.py a3: F1 held (refchk fail), bound(ref)=None, c1 inputs {'input:ref': 'F1'}, X1 label ok, accepted, published T2. a4: F1 invalidated after the check, bound(ref)=F2, X1 still ok and accepted. Model lines 859-869 and 878-884 check only that the key set matches and that upstream inputs equal the consumed version.

findings.claim: The model and the spec disagree on what counts as the same side effect for check attempts. Control 3 keys it on check x criterion x target. The model compares the full check identity, which includes the resolved check inputs, so a new check attempt of the same check x criterion x target is admitted while an earlier one is unknown. Derivation stays conservative, because pending_check_attempts makes the checks 'missing', but admission does not follow the rule. Control 8 asks for such discrepancies to be reported rather than resolved by picking a side.
findings.element: Control 3 'unknown' bullet vs model admit() side-effect loop
findings.evidence_text: attacks.py a5: c2 is admitted for (chkA, crit1, X1) after the ref step is recomputed, while c1 is in state unknown. Model lines 1250-1253 compare identity for SPECIAL_STEPS.

suggested_obligations: Under M2/M3 the human confirms the first contract, but a later deliverable on a newly added checked step, with checks chosen by the agent, takes effect automatically and can be published on its own. Review whether per-deliverable publish of such added deliverables is acceptable (Control 1.2 'N may add ... deliverables', Control 5.4).
Review whether checked steps used only as check inputs, and unchecked steps used as check inputs, need their own currency or ok conditions (to be read together with Methods 2.2-2.5).
